context: quay-crane power & yard-electrical led · marine civil is the enabler, not the driver

brief.intro: New to this project type? A container terminal is a marine civil structure — a quay wall and a heavy-duty paved yard — built to carry a small number of very powerful, very expensive machines: ship-to-shore (STS) quay cranes and yard cranes (RTG or RMG) that move containers between ship, stack and gate. The quay wall and dredging are a major early package, but once the yard is formed the schedule shifts almost entirely to electrical: getting high-voltage power, crane bus-bar/festoon feed, and reefer (refrigerated container) power distribution installed, energised and proven. Crane fabrication and delivery lead time is usually the single biggest date on the programme.

glossary.plain: ship-to-shore crane — the large quay crane that loads and unloads containers directly from the ship.
rubber-tyred or rail-mounted gantry cranes that stack and retrieve containers in the yard.
a refrigerated shipping container; reefer racks supply it with power while stacked in the yard.
the power-delivery method that keeps a moving crane continuously energised as it travels its rail.
terminal operating system — the software that plans and tracks every container move.

must_get_right: Crane fabrication and delivery is the longest lead item on the project — order STS and yard cranes before the quay wall or yard pavement design is even frozen if possible.
The quay wall and crane rail are a fixed structural interface — coordinate pile positions and rail gauge with the crane supplier early; a late change is very costly.
Electrical power to the cranes and reefer racks, not the marine structure, is what most often controls the finish date once civil works are complete.
Custody-transfer-grade instrumentation (weightometers, if fitted) and TOS integration need real calibration and acceptance time, not just a functional test.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are tied to berth and yard-block sections; the network is calculated (F9) with total float kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Marine civil (dredging, piling) often runs continuous shifts weather-permitting; yard pavement and electrical works run a standard 6-day week; crane erection needs dedicated heavy-lift weather windows and is scheduled as discrete events, not a continuous calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs dredging/quay wall → yard pavement & crane rail → crane delivery/erection → crane power terminate & energise → reefer & TOS proving → handover. Crane fabrication/delivery lead time and quay-wall completion are usually the two controlling constraints — name them explicitly when reviewing progress.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: A single mobilisation; the dredging permit and disposal site are secured before works start; the crane supply contract is let early enough to match crane-rail readiness; and no live-vessel operations occur during construction (greenfield or expansion phase).

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Marine plant (dredgers, piling rigs) access is via water and subject to tidal windows; heavy-lift crane erection needs a clear yard and a crane-carrying vessel berth; specialist crane-electrical commissioning engineers are scarce and typically travel with the crane supplier.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: crane delivery slippage, dredging weather or tidal delay, and cable-reel/festoon commissioning re-test loops. Schedule contingency is held immediately before crane energisation and before handover rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by berth/yard block; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for crane erection and commissioning — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
